learningObjective: Explain why one-hot cross-entropy keeps rewarding larger correct-class logit gaps while label-smoothed cross-entropy has a finite optimum at the smoothed target probability.
mediumRationale: A deterministic SVG loss slice is the smallest medium that shows the opposite behavior near complete confidence: one-hot loss keeps falling toward zero, while smoothed loss bottoms out at the target and then rises.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest mental model is the location of the optimum, not merely moving epsilon mass. The original plot fixes K = 5 and epsilon = 0.1, so the smoothed target is [0.92, 0.02, 0.02, 0.02, 0.02]. Along a symmetric prediction slice, each wrong class receives (1 - p_c)/4. Hard loss is -log(p_c); smoothed loss is -0.92 log(p_c) - 0.08 log((1 - p_c)/4). The latter is minimized at p_c = 0.92, where the prediction equals the target. At p_c = 0.99, hard loss falls to 0.010 while smoothed loss rises to 0.489 because the four wrong-class predictions have been pushed below their 0.02 targets. One-hot cross-entropy is bounded below by zero; the diverging quantity is the correct-class logit gap needed to approach its unattainable p_c = 1 optimum.

implementation.accessibility: The SVG has a linked title and complete description with the target allocation, formulas, minimum, and two comparison values. Direct curve labels, solid versus dashed strokes, a vertical guide, a diamond minimum, and printed values carry the lesson without color. The compact 360-unit viewBox has no minimum width or horizontal scrolling at 390 CSS pixels. Established theme variables preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared print rules provide a light high-contrast palette and keep the figure together.
